detailed_rack: Glacier kit, crampons and an ice axe.
Bolts are absent. Rack to #3, half set of wires, no pins. Crampons and a tool for the ice cap on the summit.
A typical rack for Rockies trad with a couple of knifeblades. Crampons and a tool may be useful depending on season but are not required.
Gear 0.2 to 3, offset nuts, extra 0.3-0.5 if wanted, 8 alpine draws and a couple of runners. Wear a helmet and carry bear spray.
Small alpine rack: about five cams from small to #2 and a few nuts. A 60 m rope covers all raps; thin static cord as backup. Bring approach shoes, axe or poles and bivy gear.
A helmet is the usual choice. A crash pad would help but has to be carried 10 miles.
Crampons, an ice axe and a glacier kit.
Crampons and one or two tools; two tools in swinging position add security on the bulges. If carrying a rope, take many pickets and perhaps some rock gear for running belays.
Pickets, ice screws and ice axes. Rope for glacier travel and for technical steep snow and alpine ice. Clothing, food and fuel must suit a multiple-week expedition in harsh conditions.
Bring jumars for the fixed lines. Also an ice axe, sturdy winter tent, proper clothing, stove, fuel and food.
Crampons are advisable (boot and ski), plus an axe or ice tool, or at least a whippet.
A helmet is advisable. A crash pad helps if you are willing to haul one up the mountain.
Axe and crampons are required. A rope and a skeleton rack are worth carrying if snow anchors for descending are within your skills.
Screws and pickets. A mountain axe plus one tool is handy.
Chalk and shoes with some rubber left should be enough.
Glacier gear: some pickets, crampons, ice axe. Bring skis.
Helmet and a standard rack. Crampons and ice axe are optional for the approach.

Two sets of cams from Alien green to #2 Camalot plus one #3, nuts and slings; a single 70 m rope is enough. The descent drops onto steep late-summer glacier ice: carry axe and crampons, axe alone in good snow.
Cams and nuts, one of each size to 4". Bring knifeblades and rappel webbing to back up old stations. An axe and crampons are nearly always needed.
Cams to 3", wired nuts, plus thin pins in small numbers. Axe and crampons for the descent.
Standard rack to 3". Knifeblades and lost arrows help at belays on the runout pitches. Crampons and axe for approach and descent.
Carry a full set of trad gear, small nuts through a 3 inch cam. Crampons and an ice axe may be useful for the approach and descent.
Ice axe, crampons and glacier kit.
Anyone short of a confident 5.7 leader should carry a rope and light rack. During early season an axe can come in handy for snow on the way in and out.
Two tools help on the snow bulges; one ice axe works but is less secure.
Rack to 3 inches with some doubles and a skinny 60 m rope, or half ropes with doubles; plenty of quickdraws and alpine draws. Approach shoes preferred; axe and light crampons or microspikes if snow.
Complete rack up to 4". Crampons may help on the approach and in the southeast couloir if snow remains.
Cams up to #3 Camalot, a full set. Permanent snow on the approach calls for stiff boots to kick steps and/or crampons.
Cams to 3" (triples in finger sizes) and long slings. Stiff shoes suit the crux pitch's smearing.
Wear a helmet. Seepage is common early in the season.
Alpine rack. Carry an ice axe and crampons when coming in from the north side.
Bring crampons, an ice axe or axes, and a helmet.
Two pads are enough. Drape a blanket or jacket over the rock under the opening moves to spare your back; the landing also slopes downhill.
Alpine rack with singles and some doubles, and one 60m rope. Bring approach shoes for the descent.
Several screws, red through blue sizes, with a directional at the top. Carry avalanche rescue gear (beacon, shovel, probe).
Stoppers, a single set of cams from 0.5" to 3", and many slings to cut rope drag. An ice axe may help early in the season.
Carry a single cam set plus one or two nut sets. A helmet is essential.
For rappelling and belaying, bring one 60m rope, nuts, and four or five cams in the .5 to 3 inch range. Pack plenty of slings, plus cord, for the rappels. Sturdy approach shoes suffice.
Deep water lies below. Be sure you can fall safely and have good body awareness.
Doubles from small sizes through #3, plus one #4. Bring tape or crack gloves.
Twins, a full set of nuts, a few cams from 0.5 to 2 inches, and many single and double slings. Helmets are required.
Crampons and an ice axe. Snowshoes will not work on the steep upper slope.
Two sets from tiny to #3 and one #4. Include RPs and nuts, offsets especially. Crampons may help if snow lies at the base.
Small rock rack. Early season, bring crampons plus an axe for ice. Late summer and fall: add two ice tools and several screws for ice.
Crampons and an axe are needed early in the season. The route is said to become ice as the year goes on.
Singles from #0.2 to #3, with doubles of #0.75 to #2 optional. Bring alpine draws. A helmet is essential on the approach pitch.
Winter calls for an ice ax and crampons. After or during heavy snowfall the ridge can hold cornices, deep drifts and ice, and a fall would be long. Climbers should have basic mountaineering skills.
A basic light mountaineering kit; skis allow a quick descent.

Climbed solo with an ice axe and second tool each; a standard axe may do in plenty of snow. No protection needed, though pickets and a small alpine rack may help with a beginner. Helmets and crampons are required.
An ice tool may be useful from late summer into autumn.

Start very early, when the snow is hard and icy; crampons and an ice axe are needed. The gully rarely loses its snow, but if bare it is steep, nasty talus and not recommended. A rope is often advised for the upper headwall but may not be needed.
Ice axe, crampons and helmet.
Bring an alpine rack; a rope is optional and there is no fixed protection. For the final gully, an ice axe, crampons or both may be needed, depending on conditions and experience.
Singles to #2, nuts, and 1-2 pickets for rope management around corners in neve or summer conditions. In fall bring 8-12 ice screws. Crampons and two ice tools.
Can be soloed, or use a 9mm rope and a light passive rack. In early season an ice axe helps.
Cams to about 4 inches, doubles from .75 to 2 inches, two sets of nuts and some big hexes. Getting to the wall base may call for ice axes and perhaps crampons.
Singles from .3 to #2 and alpine slings. A brush is advised, as the route is not fully cleaned.
Bring a helmet, an ice axe and crampons.
Carry crampons and an ice axe. Skis suit the approach and descent, and the ridge skis well in good conditions.
Crampons, trekking poles and one or more ice axes.

Sections of 5th class are brief: a thin rope (100 feet is plenty), a handful of cams (five or six, BD 0.4 up to #2 or #3) and two slings or so should do. An ice axe may be needed, depending on snowpack.
Light rock rack for alpine use, a BD #4 for the eastern spire, plus cordage or webbing. Bring an axe and crampons for the couloir.
Alpine rack; a 50-60m rope is optional. There are no fixed anchors. Carry an ice axe if the chute or descent holds snow.
Ice axe and crampons. With a rope, bring one set of cams and nuts, perhaps a few pitons, plus a selection of screw lengths when conditions need them.
A helmet, plus an axe and crampons, are required.
Double rack to #3 Camalot, plus stoppers. Belays are mostly on gear. The wall is north to northwest facing; wear a helmet, as the area sees little traffic.
Depending on conditions: crampons, an axe, poles, snowshoes and avalanche precautions.

Pack some nuts and cams for anchors, a light rope, and slings to back up rappel anchors. An ice axe and/or crampons suit the couloir descent. The leader of the top block wants rock shoes; the rest can wear approach shoes.
A standard alpine rack. Early in the season, carry mountain boots and an axe for ice. A few old pins remain on the route.
For the first part, an axe and crampons. For the second, a small alpine rack, with slings for moving together along the ridge.
Twins, a full set of nuts, a few cams from 0.5 to 2 inches, and slings. A helmet is required.
Carry a full RMNP alpine rack, since pitches are long. Cams suit the uniform cracks; one party took 12 slings, 6 draws, 12 cams to #3, nuts and hexes. Take an axe and crampons.
Crampons, a helmet, and a pair of tools. The left branch might call for a short rope plus an alpine rack kept light, with a few screws.
Take a 60m rope, spare rappel slings and rings, a few stoppers, and cams up to 2 inches. Wear sticky-rubber approach shoes or carry light rock shoes.
Two of each cam up to #2 or #3, plus one #4. In early season an ice axe helps.

Possibly excessive: two sets of RPs up through 3 inch cams, one 3.5 and one 4 inch cam, and extra wires. The leader should carry a nut tool. Two ropes are needed to rappel from Broadway. Wear a helmet.
Bring crampons plus an ice axe. The soloist saw no need to haul a rope in.
Crampons and axes are enough. Some smooth rock sections need technical moves that rock protection could cover; ice screws are unlikely to be useful.
Bring nuts and cams, with two of each in hand sizes (#1 to #3 Camalots), plus a #4 Friend. Having tape gloves would help.
Ice axe, crampons and helmet.
An ice or mountaineering axe.
Several pickets (24 inch length works well), sometimes a couple of screws depending on season. Crampons are needed late, when the top is ice. Rock offers little for tri-cams.
Carry an axe, crampons, and a light alpine set of gear plus long slings (several). Short ice screws (two or so) and a picket might help. Helmet advised.

Nuts 3-10 and cams 0.3-3, one each. For the aid, slings and a converted double/cordalette suffice; etriers, fifis or daisies would probably be more than two A1 moves need. Footwear can be lightweight boots made for mountains, or else approach shoes.
Carry avalanche gear (beacon, shovel, probe) and partners. Beyond axes and crampons, snow pickets or perhaps some rock gear could work, since the cliff called Black Wall sits immediately left.
Crampons and a mountaineering axe; an additional ice tool may be useful on the steps of ice.
A left-hand scree slope can bypass the ice, if you prefer not to belay it. Take rock gear if linking onto the north ridge. Two axes were handy from about a third up.
One rack of cams plus nuts. Depending on the season, crampons and/or an axe may be needed for the snowfield below the buttress.
One rack up to 3". A piolet with crampons is welcome on the approach and on the snow high in the Dragontail Couloir.
Bolts to links. The gully is quite loose in places, so consider a helmet.
Ice axes sized to the climber's comfort, crampons, and a helmet.
No rock protection is available. Bring a helmet, ice axe and crampons.
An axe, crampons and a helmet.
Axes (as comfort allows), crampons and a helmet.
Ice screws and a rope. A second rope may come in handy for rappelling. Snowshoes needed on the approach suggest it is most likely a snow climb.
Wires, cams from blue Alien up to #3.5 Camalot (or a #4 Friend), perhaps a few hexes, and a dozen 24-inch slings with extras. An ice axe is optional, a helmet essential, warm layers advisable.
Carry an ice axe. Crampons might be worth packing when the snow demands them.
Rocks and water lie below. Think about guarding against the rocks and about hypothermia from the water.

Skiers bring a whippet; snowboarders bring an axe. High on the route the slope is steep enough that a slip could prove fatal in some conditions, and a thin crust can let a whippet pull straight through.
Two sets of stoppers and doubled cams to 3 inch. Nearly every piece wants a long runner. Wear a helmet.
Pads, plus a styrofoam cup. Carry a headlamp, as the start may need one.
Helmet, crampons and tools for ice. Protecting the crux should need a short rope and nuts, perhaps with a stubby screw.
Helmet, crampons, plus axes or tools as comfort dictates. Pitching it out is not recommended; pickets would give solid protection in good conditions.
QDs and a small assortment of Camelots. Wear helmets. Bring mountaineering gear if conditions call for it.
On snow, an axe and crampons are probably wanted.
Quickdraws and Camalots C3 through #3. Most stations hold a single bolt, which most people consider enough. Pitch 5 might feel wild and somewhat scary. Wear a helmet.
Boots in good shape, plus crampons and an ice axe.
Helmet, ice axe, crampons and avalanche gear. A light technical kit may be nice: a skinny rope, snow anchors and a light rock rack. Skiing it is also an option.

Ice reportedly can form in the couloir. One party brought a mountaineering ax plus a single technical tool and never used the tool; a tool could be very handy with firmer snow or if ice appears. Crampons are a must.
A few medium nuts, cams from small (C3 sizes) up to hand-sized, plus lots of slings. Avoiding pitch 1 only needs sturdy boots and, if gullies still hold snow, an ice axe.
Pitons, snow pickets, cams and nuts were used; take a lot of slings. One party wore crampons the whole way with two tools.

Bring quickdraws for the bolts and pitons that protect every pitch up to good anchors. A light set of medium nuts and micro-cams up to a #2 Camalot ought to be enough. Mountain boots are useful, and so is an ice axe or else ski poles, depending on conditions.
12 quickdraws and shoulder runners; Camalots from micro to #1 are optional extras. All belays bolted except optional P11. Bring a helmet, rain jacket and extra warm layer.
Alpine rack. Crampons helped on the approach to the face.

The only fixed gear is the bolts atop pitch 1. One party used one nut set and cams to #3 BD, and recommends several runners of double or triple length to cut rope drag. Rock shoes were worn; the walk to and from camp crosses snow (Teepe Glacier), so plan footwear.
Two sets from fingers up to #3, a few small TCUs, one #4 and lots of long runners. Season may dictate carrying an ice axe and perhaps crampons may make sense.
Cams ranging from green alien to gold camalot (doubled), a blue cam, a 4" cam, and a set of nuts. Natural anchors throughout. An ice axe is definitely needed for the approach; crampons might be.
Regular Teton rack with some large cams. In early season an axe for the approach would be wise, and rock beneath the first roof likely stays wet then.
A Teton rack to 2" is fine. An ice axe may be needed early or midway through the season.
Wires, large nuts, and one cam set with extra 0.75s and 2.0s. A 4 would work too, but is optional. Ice axes and crampons are needed on the ascent and descent in early season or snowy years.
Standard gear is plenty. Early in the season, bring an ice axe for the couloir.
A light Teton rack up to 2". Long slings are a good idea, and so are additional long slings at rappel stations. Necessary: ice axe, crampons and helmet.
Regular gear should be enough; crampons and an axe would also be very helpful.

The crux, easy 5th class, may stay wet with seepage into midsummer; some may therefore carry nuts and a couple of mid-size cams, plus a 30m rope (short). Most solo. For the snow, which is moderate, bring crampons and an axe.
Bring several pads for the highballs, which have perfectly flat landings. Bring a stick brush.

Protection to 3", and the route has some fixed pins. Gloves of tape are not really needed, though they can help on the 5.8 variant with a fist crack near the top. One rope is enough (one party used 60 m). The party saw no bail stations along the route.

One party went ropeless, each carrying two 50 cm traditional ice axes and crampons. Belay points might exist in the rock, and anchors in snow could be used, but placing gear and belaying could put you in more danger.
Ice axe; a second tool is recommended, though not required.
Bring an ice axe plus crampons or micro spikes.
Standard gear, plus an axe for ice and possibly crampons as conditions dictate.

Nuts are recommended, plus cams (1-2 sets) running from finger size to about 3 inches. Anchors must be built at each belay; random pitons and stoppers of variable quality are fixed in a few places. 60 meter ropes help on long pitches. Carry plenty of water.

Needs depend on season, conditions and comfort with mixed ground. At a minimum: a couple mid-length screws, several small to medium nuts, perhaps 2-4 small cams to Camalot 1. Short pickets if simul-climbing low down. Ice axe and crampons are mandatory.
Double rack of .2-3, kbs, offset nuts, and beaks in medium and large sizes. Early to midsummer, add an ice axe plus steel crampons.
Ice axe and crampons. Possibly some rock pieces.
Standard gear; carry an ice axe early in the season.

For the original line, the best snow is flat, in May and June. The low ball arete that is hard lands easily. In dry conditions bring more pads. From July onward, climb it on top rope only. Early in the season a snow shovel is handy.
Gear needs run from none up through snow-climbing equipment and beyond, varying with the season and circumstances.
what_to_bring: Extra layer or durable pants for glissading
Stove and fuel for melting snow
beta: From Helen Lake, climb straight up Avalanche Gulch on snow, heading between the dark rock of The Heart on the left and Thumb Rock on the right. The slope steepens toward the Red Banks, the band of reddish volcanic cliffs at around 12,800 ft and the crux of the route. Most parties climb one of the steep snow or ice chutes that cut through the Red Banks; others go right toward Thumb Rock and climb around the end of the Red Banks, which is more exposed to the ridge and wind. Above the Red Banks, a short climb leads to the base of Misery Hill (about 13,000 ft and up), a long, tiring slope that feels like a false summit. From its top, cross the flat summit plateau and scramble up the small rocky summit pinnacle.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water; little is available above the mine ruins
Snacks for a long day above treeline
beta: Trail to South Arapaho: follow the Arapaho Pass trail to the Fourth of July Mine ruins, then switch back northeast on the signed Arapaho Glacier trail. It climbs steadily above treeline to the saddle southeast of South Arapaho, where the trail ends and a rocky, loose Class 2 scramble past a false summit leads to the top. The traverse: from South Arapaho's summit, follow the connecting ridge north, about three quarters of a mile one way. Almost all of it is Class 3, with roughly 300 ft of downclimbing and 400 ft of climbing each way, including a somewhat exposed Class 3 downclimb of about 50 ft early on. Stay near the crest and escape to the west side at difficulties; the east side drops to the glacier. Occasional painted marks and cairns show the line but are sparse. The crux: about three quarters of the way to North Arapaho, two short steps of roughly 8-10 ft each go at Class 4 on good holds; some parties find a line that stays Class 3. Final slopes: easier ground, sometimes with a lingering snow patch, leads to North Arapaho's broad summit. Allow at least an hour each way on the ridge.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water - little reliable water above the amphitheater
Gloves for scrambling on rough rock
beta: From the saddle at about 13,000 ft, follow the ridge crest and ledges on its right side. Near 13,300 ft the route crosses a small gap in the ridge, the "leap of faith" - a short step across rather than a true leap - onto narrow, exposed ledges beyond. Around 13,400 ft you reach a steep band of greenish rock (the "green wall"); climb it on Class 3-4 ledges, testing every hold. Above, the route works up a series of gullies and ledges on the west side of the ridge, marked by cairns; staying on the cairned line keeps the difficulty at Class 3-4, while wandering usually lands you on steeper, looser ground. Above about 13,900 ft the angle eases and you walk to the summit. Note landmarks on the way up, because the upper route is easy to lose on the way down.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water (none at the trailhead)
beta: From the Rock of Ages saddle, head east across a loose, rugged slope to the small saddle between Wilson Peak and Gladstone Peak. From there, traverse the south side of the ridge on Class 3 ledges and climb up to the southwest ridge at around 13,550 ft. Follow the ridge, mostly on a faint path just right of the crest, to a false summit at about 13,900 ft. From the false summit, downclimb roughly 50 ft into a notch, then scramble across stacked blocks and ledges through a prominent gash in the ridge and make the final exposed Class 3 moves to the summit. Take your time on the downclimb; it is the most exposed part of the route and is harder to reverse on the way back.

rack: Short rope and a light rack (optional, for the slab)
beta: Start at the base of the obvious slab at the foot of the peak, in the bowl between Hardscrabble and Sacagawea. The slab is the crux: roughly 50 m of easy fifth-class climbing at about 55 degrees on good rock, but it is steep and continuous enough that a fall would not stop, so climb it deliberately or rope up. Above the slab, follow the rib that runs between two gullies for roughly 175 m at a gentler angle, mostly 3rd and 4th class, staying on the crest rather than dropping into the loose gullies on either side. The rib tops out near the summit ridge; a short ridge walk leads to the summit.
